series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator to allow callers to act on the folio before it becomes visible to reclaim. This change is necessary for two users: refault evaluation and zswap writeback dropbehind.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Approved the patch with a Reviewed-by tag. No technical concerns were raised.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Sep 11, 2026 at 8:15 PM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:
>
> This is a preparatory patch.
>
> __swap_cache_alloc_folio() adds the new folio to the LRU itself, which
> leaves its callers no way to act on the folio before it becomes visible
> to reclaim.  Two users need exactly that:
>
>  - moving the refault evaluation out of the swap cache folio allocation
>    requires it to happen before folio_add_lru(): that consumes PG_active
>    to file the folio on the inactive or the active list, and under MGLRU

>  - zswap writeback dropbehind needs the buffer folio to stay off the LRU

>    keep remove_mapping() from freeing it once writeback completes.
>
> Defer the LRU insertion to the callers of __swap_cache_alloc_folio():
> each of them adds the folio right after the allocation, so there is no
> functional change intended.
>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's swap handling to drop PG_dropbehind folios from the swap cache immediately after writeback completion, rather than waiting for reclaim to find them later. This change is similar to how file folios are handled and ensures that swap cache folios are properly cleaned up when they are no longer needed. The patch adds a new function `swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio` to handle this task and modifies several other functions in the kernel's memory management code to use this new function.

review_comments.author: Alexandre Ghiti
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that the swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio() function may sleep, which could lead to a deadlock if called from folio_end_writeback(), and requested that the lock be dropped before calling try_to_unmap().

Reviewer Alexandre Ghiti noted that zswap writeback folios are not on LRU because adding them to LRU at allocation prevents remove_mapping() from freeing the folio due to a reference held by the percpu LRU cache, and suggested using folio_lock() instead of folio_trylock() to allow sleeping and ensure sleepable context.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Barry,

On Mon, Sep 14, 2026 at 1:01 AM Barry Song <baohua@kernel.org> wrote:

---

The thing is the zswap writeback folios are not on lru: that's because
if we put them on lru at allocation, the perpcu lru cache holds a
reference and it prevents remove_mapping() from freeing the folio (I
measured that with on-lru folios, the freed rate collapses from 99.9%
to ~3%).

So if we use the folio_trylock() approach, we'd need to put the folio
back on lru otherwise it would be "lost". But I don't think we can do
that while someone else holds the folio lock.

That's why I use folio_lock() which can sleep and then needs the
sleepable context.

What do you think?

Thanks,

Alex

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in the zswap writeback mechanism by dropping cold folios via swap dropbehind, reducing unnecessary reclaim scans and keeping cold memory resident for longer than necessary.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Approved the patch with a Reviewed-by tag, indicating that it meets kernel coding standards and is suitable for inclusion in the mainline kernel.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Sep 11, 2026 at 5:17 AM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:
>
> zswap writeback decompresses an entry into a fresh swap cache folio and
> writes it back. The folio is cold by construction, yet it is left on the
> LRU for reclaim to find and free later, wasting a reclaim scan and keeping
> cold memory resident longer than necessary.
>
> Allocate the folio off the LRU and mark it PG_dropbehind so the swap
> dropbehind path frees it from the swap cache once writeback completes.
>
> __swap_cache_alloc_folio() evaluates a refault on the new folio, and
> workingset_refault() sets PG_active when it looks recent. Until now
> folio_add_lru() consumed that flag and __page_cache_release() cleared it
> once the folio left the LRU. This folio never reaches the LRU, so nothing
> would clear PG_active and the folio would be freed with a
> PAGE_FLAGS_CHECK_AT_FREE flag set, tripping bad_page() under
> CONFIG_DEBUG_VM. Clear it after allocation.
>
> That is a workaround: the refault should not be evaluated on a writeback
> buffer at all. A fix for that is on the mailing list [1].
>
> Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20260911092012.92399-1-alex@ghiti.fr/ [1]
> Suggested-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>
> Suggested-by: Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com>
> Reviewed-by: Kunwu Chan <kunwu.chan@gmail.com>
> Signed-off-by: Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/2] mm/mempolicy: use SRCU for the weighted interleave state
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the weighted interleave state in the Linux kernel's memory policy module to use SRCU (Schedulable RCU) instead of copying it into a scratch array on every call. This change allows for more efficient handling of concurrent access and reduces the need for synchronization, making the code more scalable and reliable.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/2] mm/mempolicy: stop copying the nodemask in the interleave paths
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the unnecessary copying of a nodemask in interleave node selectors to improve performance and reduce memory usage. The original copy was intended to prevent division by zero and overrunning the allocation request buffer, but it did not correct distribution accuracy during rebinds. Instead, the patch introduces bounds checking for the walk and relies on the nodelist access being racy but safe. It also removes an unused function and reduces stack usage in three functions.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to eliminate unnecessary copies of nodemask and node weights in the interleave paths, improving performance by reducing memory allocation and synchronization overhead.

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: Updated mm-unstable to the latest version of the patch series.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 17 Sep 2026 20:12:01 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

> The interleave node selectors and bulk allocators take copies of
> nodemasks and node weights (for weighted interleave) in the fault path.
> Both of these copies can be entirely eliminated.
> 
> For node weights, use SRCU to pin the weights in place.  This eliminates
> a copy and a kmalloc from the bulk allocator path.
> 
> For nodemasks, we can operate directly on pol->nodes as long as we bounds
> check the walk.  A concurrent rebind can shrink the mask, or tear the read
> of it so the mask appears empty.
> 
>  - The interleave node selectors fall back to numa_node_id() when that
>    happens, which is what they already did when a copy came back empty.
> 
>  - The bulk allocator simply returns what it managed to allocate.
> 
> The node count and weight totals are read separately from the nodemask
> walk that consumes them - creating a time-of-check / time-of-use race.
> Just clamp the walk to a single pass (number of nodes), and clamp each
> bulk allocation chunk to the space left in the request.
> 
> The cost is distribution accuracy during a rebind.  The copies never
> corrected for that either - they only kept the code from dividing by
> zero and overrunning the allocation request.

Thanks, I updated mm-unstable to this version.

> v2: Comments and commit message [David]

Here's how v2 altered mm.git:


 mm/mempolicy.c |   11 +++++++++--
 1 file changed, 9 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

--- a/mm/mempolicy.c~b
+++ a/mm/mempolicy.c
@@ -2231,8 +2231,13 @@ static unsigned int weighted_interleave_
 
 	/*
 	 * The target was calculated in a separate loop, and a concurrent
-	 * rebind can change the total number of nodes.  Clamp this loop to
-	 * a single pass (nnodes) to keep the walk bounded by node count.
+	 * rebind can change the contents of pol->nodes as we calculate.
+	 * Access is safe, in the worst case we suddenly perceive an empty
+	 * nodemask and return numa_node_id() below - otherwise we may
+	 * simply cause a skew in allocations.
+	 *
+	 * Clamp this loop to a single pass (nnodes) to keep the walk
+	 * bounded by node count.
 	 */
 	while (target && nnodes-- && nid < MAX_NUMNODES) {
 		/* detect system default usage */
@@ -2266,6 +2271,8 @@ static unsigned int interleave_nid(struc
 		return numa_node_id();
 	target = ilx % nnodes;
 	nid = first_node(pol->nodes);
+
+	/* A concurrent cpuset rebind may cause us to see an empty nodemask */
 	for (i = 0; i < target && nid < MAX_NUMNODES; i++)
 		nid = next_node_in(nid, pol->nodes);
 
_

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/4] mm: support promotion-only NUMA hinting scans
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new feature to the Linux kernel's NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) balancing system called 'promotion-only' hinting scans. The goal is to optimize page placement for memory tiering systems by allowing the scanner to distinguish between placement and promotion-only scans. A new flag, MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY, is added to indicate that a protection walk should only promote pages rather than placing them. This change preserves existing behavior for certain fixes related to NUMA balancing. The patch modifies several kernel files, including mm.h, sched/fair.c, huge_memory.c, internal.h, mempolicy.c, and mprotect.c.

for definitely-not-normal-files, though with the intent of disabling

For read-only files, as David notes, we do something _weird_:

unsigned long do_mmap(struct file *file, unsigned long addr,
			unsigned long len, unsigned long prot,
			unsigned long flags, vma_flags_t vma_flags,

			...
		case MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE:
			...
			if (!(file->f_mode & FMODE_WRITE))
				vma_flags_clear(&vma_flags, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT,
						VMA_SHARED_BIT);
			...
		}
		...
	}
	...
}

So they become !VMA_SHARED_BIT, !VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT. So it's good you don't
check VMA_SHARED_BIT :)

If you map a read-only file MAP_PRIVATE as readable/writeable they will
actually have VMA_WRITE_BIT, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT set because the writes CoW
instead.

Anyway, I'm guessing what you want here is:

- Exclude MAP_PRIVATE mappings
- Cannot in any universe write to the damn thing

Which seems like you'd want to test:

In which case the test should be something like:

	return vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT) &&
		!vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT);

keep VMA_SHARED_BIT) and write-sealing a memfd gives you VMA_SHARED &&
!VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT (which is what vma_is_shared_maywrite() is for for

/**
 * vma_maps_shared_readonly_file() - Is @vma a shared mapping of a read-only
 * file?
 * @vma: The VMA to check.
 *
 * Upon mapping a read-only file with MAP_SHARED[_VALIDATE] mmap() will clear
 * VMA_SHARED_BIT and VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT.
 *
 * The VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT is retained to differentiate against mappings mapped
 * with MAP_PRIVATE.
 *
 * Some drivers clear VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT but by convention retain VMA_SHARED_BIT.
 * This is also true for write-sealed memfd's.
 *
 * Returns: true if the VMA is a shared mapping of a read-only file or false,
 * otherwise.
 */
static inline bool vma_maps_shared_readonly_file(const struct vm_area_struct *vma)
{
	/* Shared mappings of read-only files clear VMA_SHARED_BIT. */
	if (vma_test(vma, VMA_SHARED_BIT))
		return false;

	/* But MAP_SHARED mappings retain VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT. */
	if (!vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT))
		return false;

	/* Shared mappings of read-only files also clear VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT. */
	VM_WARN_ON_ONCE(vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT));

	return true;
}

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] sched/numa: do not let VMA PID activity gate promotion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents VMA PID activity from gating promotion in the NUMA scheduling algorithm. It does this by allowing periodic scans of inactive VMAs, even if they have not been recently accessed. This change is necessary to prevent starvation of placement scans and ensure that memory is properly tiered. The patch also introduces a new field to track the sequence ID of socket-placement scans. With this change, a large shmem VMA was no longer skipped during scanning, resulting in more efficient memory usage on a system with 768 GB of DRAM and 256 GB of CXL memory running two database workloads.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in NUMA balancing by separating promotion-only scans from socket-placement scans. The current implementation prevents hot memory in read-only file mappings and VMAs without recent PID activity from being promoted to a faster tier, leading to increased request latencies. The patches introduce a new protection flag (MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY) that allows for promotion-only scans, enabling eligible shared folios to be promoted and reducing the impact of filters on memory-tier promotion. This change improves performance by allowing hot memory to be moved to faster tiers, resulting in increased bandwidth usage and reduced request latencies.

review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 10 Sep 2026 20:18:22 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

> NUMA balancing uses hinting faults for both task placement and memory-tier
> promotion. Several filters designed to avoid unproductive socket-placement
> faults can also prevent promotion.
> 
> Read-only file mappings and VMAs without recent PID activity may never be
> scanned, while lower MM layers reject some shared folios. Hot memory in
> these mappings can therefore remain on a slow tier indefinitely.
> 
> Separate promotion-only scans from socket-placement scans.
> 
> MM_CP_PROT_NUMA_PROMO_ONLY carries that choice for one protection walk, so
> the PTE and PMD paths can restrict hinting faults to promotion candidates.
> Keeping this transient state in the protection flags avoids per-mm state and
> its associated lifetime, concurrency, and VMA identity problems.
> 
>   - Allow eligible shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier.
>   - Scan read-only file mappings and PID-inactive VMAs for promotion
>     without re-enabling placement sampling.
>   - Track the last placement scan separately so promotion-only scans
>     cannot postpone the existing placement-starvation fallback.
> 
> The series is ordered as follows:
> 
>   1. Add promotion-only NUMA protection walks without changing behavior.
>   2. Permit eligible shared folios to be promoted to a fast tier.
>   3. Scan read-only file mappings using promotion-only scans.
>   4. Scan PID-inactive VMAs for promotion and account for placement scans
>      separately.
> 
> Tested on a host with 768GB/256GB DRAM/CXL.
> Ran 2 ~430GB database workloads with large (>300GB) shmem VMAs.
> 
> Before change:
>   - 150-200GB/s DRAM bandwidth usage
>   - 40-45GB/s CXL bandwidth usage (maxed out)
>   - request latencies over 5ms (longer tails)
> 
> After chage:
>   - 250GB/s+ sustained DRAM bandwidth usage
>   - ~10GB/s sustained CXL bandwidth usage
>   - request latencies 800us-2ms.
> 
> Functional observation:
>   A 20 GB hash table VMA that previously remained entirely on CXL was
>   split evenly between DRAM and CXL after the changes - and tier

Here are my experiments with using IBS for memory access profiling:

1. My very early attempt was to replace NUMA hint faults with IBS
provided memory access information to drive NUMA Balancing. This
worked for all the modes of NUMA Balancing (kernel.numa_balancing=1
or 2) [1]

2. The next attempt was to use IBS data to drive only hot page promotion.
In this approach, IBS was used as one of the sources of page hotness
information to pghot (existing NUMA hintfaults being the other) [2]

Both the above approaches used the primary IBS instance that was being
used by perf sub-system also and I had made the use mutually exclusive.

> 
> I'm not sure there's been proposals for better hardware support.

Then AMD Zen6 processors introduced a 2nd light-weight IBS instance
called IBS Memory Profiler which is separate, works independently
of the primary IBS instance (which continues to be used by perf)
and which is primarily targeted for memory access profiling.

I have used this as source of page hotness with pghot (pghot-hwhints)
and the benchmark results are encouraging. [3]

Also it is worth reiterating here that neither primary IBS nor this
new IBS Memory Profiler have got anything to do with PMU sub-system.

In this context, I would also like to point out that pghot patchset [4]
is trying to move hot page promotion from scheduler to its own dedicated
sub-system. I have done the following till now:

- Extracted out hot page promotion engine and moved it to pghot
  so that the same gets used for other sources of page hotness.
- Moved fault-time migration to async and batched kernel-thread driven
  migration (kmigrated)
- Used NUMA hint faults as page hotness source to pghot (pghot-hintfaults)

I have often wondered if it makes sense to move out complete hint faulting
mechanism out of scheduler but then I see that task-follows-memory part,
the scanning logic, fault stats heuristics are tightly tied to the scheduler.

Also apt is to remember the PTE-A bit scanning approach [5] that was started
as a potential replacement to NUMA hint faults based scanning. We are
planning to revive that effort and make it as another source for pghot
if we get good results with different benchmarks.

- Cannot in any universe write to the damn thing

/**
 * vma_maps_shared_readonly_file() - Is @vma a shared mapping of a read-only
 * file?
 * @vma: The VMA to check.
 *

 * VMA_SHARED_BIT and VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT.
 *

 * with MAP_PRIVATE.
 *

 * This is also true for write-sealed memfd's.
 *
 * Returns: true if the VMA is a shared mapping of a read-only file or false,
 * otherwise.
 */
static inline bool vma_maps_shared_readonly_file(const struct vm_area_struct *vma)
{
	/* Shared mappings of read-only files clear VMA_SHARED_BIT. */
	if (vma_test(vma, VMA_SHARED_BIT))
		return false;

	/* But MAP_SHARED mappings retain VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT. */
	if (!vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT))
		return false;

	/* Shared mappings of read-only files also clear VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT. */
	VM_WARN_ON_ONCE(vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT));

	return true;
}

protect from future changes that might somehow allow this could be:

	return !vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT);

 * Some drivers clear VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT but by convention retain VMA_SHARED_BIT.
 * This is also true for write-sealed memfd's.
 *
 * Returns: true if the VMA is a shared mapping of a read-only file or false,
 * otherwise.
 */
static inline bool vma_maps_shared_readonly_file(const struct vm_area_struct *vma)
{
	/* Shared mappings of read-only files clear VMA_SHARED_BIT. */
	if (vma_test(vma, VMA_SHARED_BIT))
		return false;

	/* But MAP_SHARED mappings retain VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT. */
	if (!vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYSHARE_BIT))
		return false;

	/* Shared mappings of read-only files also clear VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT. */
	VM_WARN_ON_ONCE(vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT));

	return true;
}

The assert here is because nothing else clears VMA_SHARED_BIT like this, but to
protect from future changes that might somehow allow this could be:

	return !vma_test(vma, VMA_MAYWRITE_BIT);

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 01/10] nfsdctl: sync nfsd_netlink.h with the kernel
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the nfsd_netlink.h header file in the nfs-utils package to match the latest version from the Linux kernel. It imports new attributes related to rpcbind registration, including NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_USERSPACE_RPCBIND and NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_RPCBIND, which allow a caller to own an rpcbind registration. The patch also updates the configure.ac file to use these new attributes when determining whether to use the system's netlink headers or the imported ones. This change is necessary because some systems may have older kernel versions that do not include these new attributes in their netlink headers.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 02/10] nfsdctl: probe the policy of any command
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl utility to probe the policy of any command, not just THREADS_SET. It introduces a new function query_nfsd_nl_cmd_policy() that takes the command number as an argument and writes the highest attribute through its callback argument. The existing query_nfsd_nl_policy() function is updated to call this new function with the THREADS_SET command number. This change allows multiple commands to use the getpolicy_handler() function simultaneously, without overwriting each other's results.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 03/10] nfsdctl: share the listener nest parser
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the listener parsing code in nfsdctl to share a common function for unpacking NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_ADDR nests. The original code had this logic duplicated in multiple places, which has been consolidated into a single function called parse_sock_nest(). This change improves code organization and reduces duplication, but does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 04/10] nfsdctl: add rpcbind registration helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds rpcbind registration helpers to the nfsdctl utility, which is used to manage NFS services. The helpers register and unregister NFS services with the local rpcbind service, matching each listener against kernel-reported programs. The patch also moves the struct server_socket definition to a new header file and updates Makefile.am to include the new files. The registration process is conditional on the presence of libtirpc and does not require rpcbind for NFSv4 or clients that already know the port number.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 05/10] nfsdctl: register nfsd listeners with rpcbind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl utility to register NFS and NFSACL listeners with rpcbind in a more asynchronous manner, avoiding a deadlock that occurred when a slow rpcbind blocked other NFSD netlink commands. The patch detects support for this new behavior by checking for a specific attribute in LISTENER_SET, and it clears all existing entries before registering the new ones. This approach ensures that the registration is only attempted after the reply from rpcbind has been parsed, preventing potential issues with incomplete registrations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 06/10] nfsdctl: clear rpcbind entries when the serv is torn down
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl utility to clear rpcbind entries when the NFS server is torn down. The previous behavior was inconsistent, as some paths cleared these entries while others did not. The patch fixes this by adding a check for zero threads in all pools and clearing the rpcbind entries if so. This ensures that the rpcbind entries are properly cleaned up even when the server is shut down unexpectedly or due to listener failures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 07/10] nfsdctl: add missing break in update_listeners()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the nfsdctl utility where a missing break statement caused a v4 listener to be re-tested as a sockaddr_in6, leading to incorrect behavior. The patch adds breaks at the end of each case arm in the update_listeners function to prevent fallthrough and ensure correct handling of different address families.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 08/10] nfsdctl: fix heap overflow in autostart_func() listener cleanup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a heap overflow bug in the autostart_func() function of the nfsdctl utility. The bug occurs when cleaning up listeners after one or more fail to start, causing the program to write beyond the bounds of a dynamically allocated array. To fix this, the code now sizes the array based on the number of threads specified in the /etc/nfs.conf file, rather than setting it to 0 when cleanup is necessary. Additionally, a separate bug that caused memory leaks due to an incorrect return statement has been fixed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 09/10] nfsdctl: reject a listener insertion when the table is full
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents a buffer overflow in the nfsdctl utility by rejecting listener insertions when the table is full, thus preventing an out-of-bounds memory access that could occur when trying to add more listeners than the maximum allowed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils v2 10/10] nfsdctl: check the netlink attribute puts in set_listeners()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue in the nfsdctl utility where it silently truncates listener information when sending netlink messages to the kernel, leading to EINVAL errors. The fix checks for and reports overflows of listener information within a single message, preventing truncated data from being sent.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patchset allows the nfsdctl utility to handle rpcbind registration and deregistration, rather than relying on the kernel to do so. It introduces a new NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_USERSPACE_RPCBIND flag that tells the kernel not to register with rpcbind, and instead calls out to rpcbind using libtirpc client interfaces. The patchset also includes various bug fixes and improvements to nfsdctl's functionality.

The author confirmed that failed calls write warnings but do not stop the caller, and that nfsd_rpcb_unset_all() clears every nfsd entry with nfs_svc_unregister().
review_comments.raw_body:
Add the code that calls the local rpcbind. The callers come next.

nfsd_rpcb_register() matches each listener against each program that the
kernel reported. It calls rpcb_set() for every pair.

nfsd_rpcb_unset_all() clears every nfsd entry with nfs_svc_unregister().
That helper calls rpcb_unset() with no netconfig, so one call covers
every netid.

Three rules match what the kernel did:

- nfsdctl registers the wildcard address with the listener's port. It
  does not register the address that the listener uses.
  __svc_rpcb_register4() and __svc_rpcb_register6() did the same.
- nfsdctl does not register an RDMA listener. svc_register() runs only
  from svc_setup_socket(), so an RDMA listener never reached rpcbind.
- nfsdctl does not register a program that carries the no-udp flag on
  udp or udp6. NFSv4 sets vs_need_cong_ctrl, so the kernel never
  advertised NFSv4 there.

A failed call writes a warning and does not stop the caller. NFSv4 does
not need rpcbind. A v2 or v3 client that already knows the port does not
need it either.

rpcb_set() and the netconfig database are TI-RPC only, so the
registration side sits under HAVE_LIBTIRPC with a warning stub, matching
getport.c and rpc_socket.c. nfsd_rpcb_unset_all() needs neither and
stays unconditional; nfs_svc_unregister() has a pmap_unset() variant.

struct server_socket moves to the new header, because both files read it.
The netlink spec generates nfsdctl.h, so the definition cannot live
there.

+/*
+ * rpcbind.c -- register nfsd listeners with the local rpcbind
+ *
+ * A kernel that accepts NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_USERSPACE_RPCBIND makes no
+ * rpcbind call of its own, so this program makes them instead. The kernel
+ * used to do this under nfsd_mutex, where a slow rpcbind stalled every
+ * other NFSD netlink operation.
+ *
+ * lockd still registers NLM itself, so nothing here touches it.
+ */

+#ifdef HAVE_CONFIG_H
+#include <config.h>
+#endif
+
+#include <errno.h>
+#include <netinet/in.h>
+#include <string.h>
+#include <sys/socket.h>
+
+#include <rpc/rpc.h>
+
+#ifdef HAVE_LIBTIRPC
+#include <rpc/rpcb_clnt.h>
+#include <netconfig.h>
+#endif	/* HAVE_LIBTIRPC */
+
+#include "nfslib.h"
+#include "rpcmisc.h"
+#include "sockaddr.h"
+#include "xlog.h"
+#include "rpcbind.h"
+
+#ifdef USE_SYSTEM_NFSD_NETLINK_H
+#include <linux/nfsd_netlink.h>
+#else
+#include "nfsd_netlink.h"
+#endif
+
+#ifndef ARRAY_SIZE
+#define ARRAY_SIZE(x)		(sizeof(x) / sizeof((x)[0]))
+#endif
+
+/*
+ * Programs to clear at shutdown. There is no reply to read at that point,
+ * so clear a superset. rpcb_unset() of an absent entry does nothing.
+ */
+static const struct {
+	rpcprog_t	program;
+	rpcvers_t	version;
+} nfsd_rpcb_all[] = {
+	{ NFS_PROGRAM,		2 },
+	{ NFS_PROGRAM,		3 },
+	{ NFS_PROGRAM,		4 },
+	{ NFS_ACL_PROGRAM,	2 },
+	{ NFS_ACL_PROGRAM,	3 },
+};
+
+/**
+ * nfsd_rpcb_unset_all - remove every nfsd entry from the local rpcbind
+ *
+ * rpcb_unset() matches [program, version, netid] and takes no address, so
+ * one call clears every netid. This mirrors the svc_unregister() sweep that
+ * svc_rpcb_setup() used to run, which an sv_no_rpcbind serv no longer does.
+ */
+void nfsd_rpcb_unset_all(void)
+{
+	unsigned int i;
+
+	for (i = 0; i < ARRAY_SIZE(nfsd_rpcb_all); i++)
+		nfs_svc_unregister(nfsd_rpcb_all[i].program,
+				   nfsd_rpcb_all[i].version);
+}
+
+#ifdef HAVE_LIBTIRPC
+
+/*
+ * Map a transport name and address family to an rpcbind netid.
+ *
+ * Returns NULL for a transport that the kernel never registered. RDMA is
+ * the case that matters: svc_register() is only reached from
+ * svc_setup_socket(), so an RDMA listener was always absent from rpcbind.
+ */
+static const char *nfsd_rpcb_netid(const char *transport, int family)
+{
+	bool v6 = (family == AF_INET6);
+
+	if (!strcmp(transport, "tcp"))
+		return v6 ? "tcp6" : "tcp";
+	if (!strcmp(transport, "udp"))
+		return v6 ? "udp6" : "udp";
+	return NULL;
+}
+
+/*
+ * Build the address to register. The kernel registered the wildcard address
+ * with the listener's port, not the address the listener is bound to, so
+ * match that.
+ */
+static bool nfsd_rpcb_wildcard(const struct sockaddr_storage *ss,
+			       struct sockaddr_storage *out, socklen_t *len)
+{
+	memset(out, 0, sizeof(*out));
+
+	switch (ss->ss_family) {
+	case AF_INET: {
+		struct sockaddr_in *s4 = (struct sockaddr_in *)out;
+
+		s4->sin_family = AF_INET;
+		s4->sin_addr.s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY);
+		s4->sin_port = ((const struct sockaddr_in *)ss)->sin_port;
+		*len = sizeof(*s4);
+		return true;
+	}
+	case AF_INET6: {
+		struct sockaddr_in6 *s6 = (struct sockaddr_in6 *)out;
+
+		s6->sin6_family = AF_INET6;
+		s6->sin6_addr = in6addr_any;
+		s6->sin6_port = ((const struct sockaddr_in6 *)ss)->sin6_port;
+		*len = sizeof(*s6);
+		return true;
+	}
+	}
+	return false;
+}
+
+static bool nfsd_rpcb_set_one(rpcprog_t program, rpcvers_t version,
+			      const char *netid,
+			      const struct sockaddr_storage *ss)
+{
+	struct sockaddr_storage wild;
+	struct netconfig *nconf;
+	struct netbuf nb;
+	socklen_t len;
+	bool ok;
+
+	if (!nfsd_rpcb_wildcard(ss, &wild, &len))
+		return false;
+
+	nconf = getnetconfigent(netid);
+	if (!nconf) {
+		xlog(L_WARNING, "no netconfig entry for %s", netid);
+		return false;
+	}
+
+	nb.buf = &wild;
+	nb.len = len;
+	nb.maxlen = len;
+
+	ok = (rpcb_set(program, version, nconf, &nb) == TRUE);
+	freenetconfigent(nconf);
+	return ok;
+}
+
+/**
+ * nfsd_rpcb_register - register the listeners the kernel reported
+ * @listeners: listeners that came up, from the listener_set reply
+ * @nlisteners: number of entries in @listeners
+ * @progs: programs and versions the kernel would have registered
+ * @nprogs: number of entries in @progs
+ *
+ * A failure is not fatal. NFSv4 does not need rpcbind, and a v2/v3 client
+ * that already knows the port does not need it either, so an unadvertised
+ * server is better than no server.
+ */
+void nfsd_rpcb_register(const struct server_socket *listeners, int nlisteners,
+			const struct nfsd_rpcb_prog *progs, int nprogs)
+{
+	unsigned int failed = 0;
+	int i, j, k;
+
+	/*
+	 * Clear first. rpcbind cannot express "drop one of two TCP ports",
+	 * and the kernel no longer sweeps stale entries at serv creation.
+	 */
+	nfsd_rpcb_unset_all();
+
+	for (i = 0; i < nlisteners; i++) {
+		const struct server_socket *l = &listeners[i];
+		const char *netid;
+		bool dup = false;
+
+		netid = nfsd_rpcb_netid(l->name, l->ss.ss_family);
+		if (!netid)
+			continue;
+
+		/*
+		 * The address registered is the wildcard, so two listeners
+		 * that share a netid and port produce the same entry.
+		 */
+		for (k = 0; k < i; k++) {
+			const struct server_socket *o = &listeners[k];
+			const char *other;
+
+			other = nfsd_rpcb_netid(o->name, o->ss.ss_family);
+			if (other && !strcmp(other, netid) &&
+			    nfs_get_port((const struct sockaddr *)&o->ss) ==
+			    nfs_get_port((const struct sockaddr *)&l->ss)) {
+				dup = true;
+				break;
+			}
+		}
+		if (dup)
+			continue;
+
+		for (j = 0; j < nprogs; j++) {
+			const struct nfsd_rpcb_prog *p = &progs[j];
+
+			/*
+			 * NFSv4 needs congestion control, so the kernel
+			 * never advertised it over UDP.
+			 */
+			if ((p->flags & NFSD_RPCBIND_FLAGS_NO_UDP) &&
+			    !strncmp(netid, "udp", 3))
+				continue;
+
+			if (nfsd_rpcb_set_one(p->program, p->version, netid,
+					      &l->ss))
+				continue;
+
+			xlog(L_WARNING,
+			     "cannot register program %u version %u on %s port %u",
+			     p->program, p->version, netid,
+			     nfs_get_port((const struct sockaddr *)&l->ss));
+			failed++;
+		}
+	}
+
+	if (failed)
+		xlog(L_WARNING,
+		     "some rpcbind registrations failed. Clients that look up the server in rpcbind cannot find it.");
+}
+
+#else	/* !HAVE_LIBTIRPC */
+
+/*
+ * rpcb_set() and the netconfig database are TI-RPC only, so a build
+ * without it cannot own the registration. userspace_rpcbind_supported()
+ * answers false there and the kernel keeps doing the calls itself, which
+ * leaves this unreachable.
+ */
+void nfsd_rpcb_register(const struct server_socket *UNUSED(listeners),
+			int UNUSED(nlisteners),
+			const struct nfsd_rpcb_prog *UNUSED(progs),
+			int UNUSED(nprogs))
+{
+	xlog(L_WARNING, "built without TI-RPC: cannot register with rpcbind");
+}
+
+#endif	/* !HAVE_LIBTIRPC */

new file mode 100644
index 000000000000..46145da6ed99
--- /dev/null
+++ b/utils/nfsdctl/rpcbind.h
@@ -0,0 +1,42 @@

+ * rpcbind.h -- register nfsd listeners with the local rpcbind
+ */
+
+#ifndef _UTILS_NFSDCTL_RPCBIND_H
+#define _UTILS_NFSDCTL_RPCBIND_H
+
+#include <stdbool.h>
+#include <stdint.h>

+#endif
+#ifndef NFS_ACL_PROGRAM
+#define NFS_ACL_PROGRAM		100227
+#endif

+/*
+ * All of the existing netids are short strings (3-4 chars), but let's allow
+ * for up to 16.
+ */
+#define MAX_CLASS_NAME_LEN	16
+
+struct server_socket {
+	struct sockaddr_storage	ss;
+	char name[MAX_CLASS_NAME_LEN];
+	bool active;
+};

+/* One [program, version] that the kernel would have registered. */
+struct nfsd_rpcb_prog {
+	uint32_t	program;
+	uint32_t	version;
+	uint32_t	flags;
+};

+void nfsd_rpcb_unset_all(void);

+			const struct nfsd_rpcb_prog *progs, int nprogs);

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in the Linux kernel's memory control module to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, mirroring the existing seven-slot representation from memcg. The new structure, struct page_counter_stock_pcp, preserves all fields and behaviors from its memcg equivalent but adds a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the base of the percpu stock and the owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this initial introduction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios in try_charge_memcg, where the goal is to charge as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots or making a greedy charge to refill the stock. The second parameter reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge, preserving existing batch-based memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more flexible management of memory usage. The change decouples the memory and memsw counters, which can temporarily diverge in value. To preserve the legacy user-visible invariant that memory usage is less than or equal to swap usage, the larger raw value between memory and memsw is reported. The patch also removes unused memcg code and preserves existing behaviors for cgroup v2 users. Future work will introduce additional page counters without removing the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v6 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), and the existing direct memsw rollback is preserved when memory charge fails. This change enables the raw counters for both banks to temporarily drift due to cached amounts, while maintaining the user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant by reporting the larger value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages, known as 'stock', from mem_cgroup to page_counter. This change is necessary to make future page_counters scalable and performant, particularly in scenarios where multiple new page_counters are introduced to a memcg. The existing seven-slot per-CPU design and drain policy are retained. For memcg v1 users, this decouples the memory and memsw stocks, potentially leading to different sizes of precharged cache for each. To prevent an invariant from being broken, the patch reports the larger value of memory and memsw usage_in_bytes for memsw reporting.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn (author)
review_comments.summary:
The author acknowledges that the asynchronous draining mechanism may lead to futile reclaim retries, but is considering it acceptable due to its lower overhead compared to synchronous reclamation. They plan to separate the code move from the draining improvements and will address this issue in a follow-up patch.

Author responded to reviewer feedback with a brief acknowledgement, but did not address any specific technical concerns or indicate plans for revision.
review_comments.raw_body:
So I was thinking about this part quite a bit in the older versions of
this series where I changed the draining from being async to sync.

If I understand the issue you saw in LTP correctly, it's not one of
actual memory OOMs but that there was stock that the memcg could use,
just not in the current CPU that was trying to fulfill the charge,
and also the draining for the remote CPUs did not happen in the time
that it took to run through 16 retry attempts.

IOW seems to me we are synchronously waiting for asynchronous drains.

To me this did sound a little bit unfortunate since there really is
memory that the memcg could have used, just cached in the "wrong"
place (and for some reason that CPU is too busy to do the drain).
One of the versions that I worked on previously (v4, [2]) used an atomic
for the stock so that we just always do a synchronous drain via
cmpxchg and we wouldn't have the problem above.

Obviously there are pros and cons. Synchronous means the reclaim path
has the ability to reclaim more memory NOW and prevent futile reclaim
retries, but also it makes each flushing operation more expensive as
the cmpxchg operation is more expensive than acquiring a local trylock,
even if it succeeds on the first try. 

In my opinion just doing the synchronous reclamation makes a bit more
sense to me since it gives a stronger guarantee that we are going to
get the charges we need to fulfill the charge attempt NOW rather than
spinning until some remote CPU gets scheduled to perform a local flush.

But this is just personal taste, I haven't really seen too much 
evidence that we are wasting too much time on the reclaims. So maybe
asynchronous drains are OK here. I can do some more digging in our
production data to see if we're ever just waiting for remote drains
to finish.

Anyways, I still intend on separating out the two efforts so that this
one is just a simple code move (and make stock more scalable) for
cgroup v2 users (and I hope not-so-big impact for cgroup v1 users)
and I can work on removing the 7-slot limit and improving the draining
as a follow-up work.

---

Thanks for your thoughts Michal. Have a great day!
Joshua

The redundant mmgrab() was being held across the work of madvise_collapse(), but since all callers to this function already hold a valid reference to the mm_struct, it can be safely dropped. This patch simplifies the code and reduces unnecessary memory management.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 02/12] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to count collapses where it makes them, allowing the daemon to keep its own counter without relying on shared paths. The change affects the collapse_single_pmd function, which now increments the khugepaged_pages_collapsed counter only when the caller is the khugepaged daemon and the collapse is successful.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 03/12] mm/khugepaged: rename mthp_present_ptes bitmap to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the 'mthp_present_ptes' bitmap in the khugepaged code to 'eligible_ptes'. The name change reflects that a set bit in this bitmap indicates not only that a PTE is present, but also that it has passed additional checks such as uffd, lazyfree, anonymity, and sharing. The patch updates comments and code accordingly without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 04/12] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the collapse interface
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new header file, mm/collapse.h, to separate the interface and state of the collapse mechanism from its implementation in khugepaged.c. The new header defines an enum for scan results and a struct for control data passed between the user and engine sides. Two constants are also moved from khugepaged.c to the new header. This change improves code organization and maintainability without introducing any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 05/12] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct collapse_policy that allows the caller to specify what actions are allowed during a memory collapse operation. The policy is used by khugepaged and MADV_COLLAPSE to determine which VMAs are eligible for collapse, how many empty or swapped-out PTEs can be included in a window, and other settings. The patch removes the need for the collapse code to look up who called it and instead relies on the caller to fill in the policy once per scan pass or call. This change simplifies the code and improves performance by reducing the number of checks performed during each table scan.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 06/12] mm/collapse: drop the collapse_possible() wrapper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the collapse_possible() function wrapper, which only forwarded to collapse_possible_orders(). The three callers of collapse_possible() can directly test the mask returned by collapse_possible_orders(), resulting in no functional change.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 07/12] mm/collapse: name the per-table scan reset for what it resets
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the function collapse_control_init_scan() to collapse_scan_reset(), which more accurately reflects its purpose of resetting accumulated data for a scan, including node load, allocation nodemask, and eligible PTE bitmap. This change is part of a larger effort to improve naming conventions in the code and prepare for future changes that will involve initialization and release functions for each control. The patch does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 08/12] mm/collapse: separate scanning a PTE table from collapsing it
series_items.patch_summary: This patch separates the scanning of a PTE table from its collapse into two distinct functions: `collapse_scan_pmd` and `collapse_run_pmd`. The scan function reads the table under the mmap_lock, while the run function performs the actual collapse. This change improves code organization and reduces the complexity of the original `collapse_single_pmd` function. Additionally, it allows for more efficient handling of file tables by khugepaged and introduces changes to tracing events.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 10/12] mm/collapse: work out the orders a VMA allows once per VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way VMA (Virtual Memory Area) orders are calculated by only doing it once per VMA instead of once per PTE table. This is done to improve performance and reduce unnecessary work. The patch also introduces a new parameter, `enabled_orders`, which is passed from the caller to the function that calculates the allowed orders for a VMA. This change allows the code to take advantage of the fact that hugepage_vma_revalidate() tests the order again under the lock the collapse retakes, making it more efficient.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 11/12] mm/collapse: declare the collapse interface in collapse.h
series_items.patch_summary: This patch declares the collapse interface in collapse.h, which includes functions and variables related to collapsing memory pages. The functions are: collapse_control_init, collapse_scan_pmd, collapse_run_pmd, and collapse_control_release. These functions are used for collapsing large pages into smaller ones. The patch also renames hugepage_vma_revalidate to collapse_vma_revalidate and adds comments to explain the order of function calls and lock usage. This is a preparation step for implementing MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c, but it does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 12/12] mm/collapse: implement MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the implementation of MADV_COLLAPSE from khugepaged.c to madvise.c, where it belongs among other madvise operations. This change simplifies the code and removes unnecessary dependencies between the daemon's file and the syscall code. The MADV_COLLAPSE operation is a caller of the interface used by khugepaged, so its functionality remains unchanged. Additionally, the !CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE stub is moved along with the implementation.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set separates the collapse engine from its callers by introducing a clear interface and policy between them. This separation allows for better modularity and maintainability of the code, as well as improved handling of lock states and policy decisions. The patch set also includes changes to madvise.c to gain a new operation and updates to various functions to follow the new interface.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

khugepaged.c holds both the users of collapse and the machinery that
performs it.  The daemon's scan loop, the sysfs tunables, MADV_COLLAPSE's
entry point and the collapse itself all sit in one file and reach into
each other freely.  Nothing marks where a user ends and the engine
begins.

Start drawing that line.

Add mm/collapse.h for what the two sides have to agree on:

  - enum scan_result - what the engine hands back;
  - struct collapse_control - the state a request carries.

And two constants move with them:

  - KHUGEPAGED_MAX_PTES_LIMIT -> COLLAPSE_MAX_PTES_LIMIT;
  - KHUGEPAGED_MIN_MTHP_ORDER -> COLLAPSE_MIN_MTHP_ORDER.

Neither is a fact about the daemon, so both lose the KHUGEPAGED_ prefix.

No functional change.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 01/11] mm, swap: add virtual swap device infrastructure
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces the virtual swap device infrastructure, which allows for dynamic allocation of swap clusters and enables the creation of a virtual swap device that can be used by vswap. The device is capped at approximately 8 TiB in size and uses a 64-bit architecture. The patch also includes changes to various kernel files to support the new infrastructure and adds a kernel parameter 'vswap' to control the behavior of the virtual swap device. The dynamic-cluster allocator is wired in, but no allocation path can select it yet, as this will be handled in subsequent patches.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 02/11] mm, swap: support zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for virtual swap (vswap) using zswap and zero-filled swap pages as backends, allowing compressed or zero-filled pages to be stored without pre-allocating physical swap space. It introduces a new vswap layer that decouples PTE swap entries from physical backing, enabling efficient compression and detection of zero-filled pages. The patch also includes changes to handle virtual swap-backed entries in the zswap shrinker and writeback paths, as well as updates to mem_cgroup_can_swap() to account for vswap's contribution to memory pressure. Additionally, it introduces a new function mem_cgroup_can_vswap() to determine whether vswap is enabled for a given cgroup.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 03/11] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the swap IO path for vswap by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. It achieves this by computing the sector from an explicit entry, which is then used in various functions such as swap_add_folio and __swap_writeout. This change enables the batching path to serve both vswap entries and physical entries mapped directly into PTEs. The patch also updates ops->can_merge to measure sectors and byte offsets from the batch head plus accumulated length instead of from the previous folio plus its size.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/11] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer, allowing zswap to allocate physical slots on demand when it declines a page. It introduces a new mechanism to track physical slots via pointer-tagged swap_table entries and modifies readahead and swapoff operations to work with this new system. The patch also includes changes to handle cases where zswap is disabled or the folio's cgroup does not support vswap, bypassing vswap and mapping the slot directly into PTEs.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 05/11] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables transparent huge page (THP) swapin for vswap entries, allowing large anonymous folios to be swapped in as a unit when their vswap entries share contiguous physical swap slots on a synchronous IO device. This change improves performance by reducing the number of faults and retries required during swap operations. The patch also introduces checks for zswap-backed or mixed-backing batches, which are still refused and fall back to order-0 faults. The approach taken involves modifying existing functions in the mm module to handle vswap entries and THP swapin.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/11] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap. It mirrors the existing zswap writeback path, but allocates the backing physical slot on demand at writeback time rather than pre-allocating it. The zswap shrinker no longer skips vswap entries unless there is no available physical swap space. The patch modifies the zswap_writeback_entry function to handle vswap entries by allocating physical backing before decompressing and storing the entry in the vtable.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 07/11] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries are not being reclaimed when they become redundant. When a vswap entry's swap_count drops to 0 while its folio is still in the swap cache, the entry becomes cache-only and its physical slot is no longer needed. However, the current implementation does not properly reclaim these slots. This patch introduces a new flag, SWP_RMAP_CACHE_ONLY, to indicate when a vswap entry is cache-only, and modifies the physical reclaim scanner to reclaim such slots once swap usage exceeds 50%. The reclaimed slots are then freed, allowing for new allocations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 08/11] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies how memory charge is handled for swap entries in Linux. It ensures that only physical swap entries are charged against a cgroup's swap, rather than all swap entries including zswap-backed and zero-filled pages. This change affects the behavior of memory.swap.current and allows cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even when memory.swap.max is set to 0. The patch also refactors the swap memcg operations into separate helpers for getting, recording, charging, uncharging, and putting swap entries.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 09/11] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track virtual swap usage in the Linux kernel. The first counter, 'used', tracks the number of virtual swap slots (pages) currently allocated. The second counter, 'alloc_reject', counts the cumulative pages that failed to get a vswap slot. These counters are exposed under the '/sys/kernel/debug/vswap/' directory and can be accessed via debugfs. This patch addresses the need for visibility into virtual swap usage statistics, which is useful for debugging and performance analysis.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 10/11] mm, swap: defer memcg_table allocation for physical swap clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory allocation for physical swap clusters by deferring the allocation of a memcg table until it is actually needed. This reduces unnecessary memory usage in cases where a cluster only holds vswap backings, which do not require a memcg table. The patch modifies the swap_cluster_alloc_table function to allocate the memcg table eagerly only when the cluster is known to be used for direct mapping or when vswap is disabled.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v5 11/11] mm, swap: back vswap clusters with a VM_SPARSE array
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the vswap cluster's individually allocated memory with a VM_SPARSE array, simplifying access and reducing overhead. The new approach eliminates per-cluster allocation, xarray nodes, and RCU grace periods, making it more efficient. The swap_cluster_info_dynamic wrapper is removed, and the virtual table for a vswap cluster is freed when it empties, reclaiming most of its memory. This change aims to improve performance and reduce memory usage in the Linux kernel's swap management.

patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Patch proposes to prevent handing out large folios above memory.high, sparking a discussion on the semantics of memory high enforcement and its interaction with THP.

review_comments.author: Shakeel Butt
review_comments.summary: Raised concerns about polluting non-memcg MM code with memcg internal details and questioned the real use-case for throttling large folios above memory.high. Asked Qinyun Tan to provide a real-world scenario where this is necessary.

review_comments.author: Qinyun Tan
review_comments.summary: Admitted to not having a real use-case for the patch and acknowledged that memory.high enforcement depends on the folio order, which is an issue. Expressed willingness to rework the patch if throttling large folios above memory.high is deemed necessary.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 9/18/26 9:26 AM, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> On Tue, Sep 15, 2026 at 12:25:46PM +0800, Qinyun Tan wrote:
>> memory.high is enforced on return to userspace, and synchronously in
> 
> Over time I feel like this sync throttle for memory.high was a bad decision but
> that is an orthogonal discussion.
> 
>> try_charge_memcg() for large overcharges, but only when the charge gfp
>> allows blocking.  A populate loop - mlock(), MADV_POPULATE_*, any
>> GUP-driven population - never returns to userspace, and large folios are
>> charged with the THP allocation gfp, which does not allow blocking under
>> the default defrag=madvise without MADV_HUGEPAGE, nor under defrag=defer.
>> So neither runs: usage grows from memory.high straight up to memory.max
>> with no reclaim and no penalty sleep.
>>
>> mlock(200M) in a cgroup with memory.high=30M and memory.max=140M.  Of the
>> 110M between high and max, the burst consumed:
>>
>>   4K pages                       3M in 5s, then still throttled
>>   THP, defrag=always             6M in 5s, then still throttled
>>   THP, defrag=madvise          110M in 13ms, then OOM killed at 16ms
>>   THP, defrag=madvise, patched   3M in 5s, then still throttled
> 
> I don't really like polluting non-memcg MM code with memcg internal details.
> Let's first discuss the semantics we want here. Please tell why getting
> oom-killed by kernel in the scenario you have described (mlock() larger than
> memory.max) is wrong. How does throttling it will help? What can the external
> observer (userspace oom-killer) do other than killing it? Or you are thinking
> that the workload itself is observing itself and change the behavior (though
> the big mlock one can't do anything).
> 
> What I am looking for is the real use-case you have for this case. Not
> mlock()ing big chunk or creating a lot of unreclaimable memory and going over
> memory.high. For example the reason I added the sync throttle in memory.high was
> to implement a feature Google has in their internal kernel where a workload hits
> its memory.max limit, kernel delays the kill for couple of seconds and during
> that time, the node controller may decide to increase the limit based on the
> memory situation of the memory. However even with sync throttle, we couldn't
> reliably implement the alternative because applications there have thousands of
> threads and there is threading library which keeps cloning more threads if it
> observes threads getting throttled.
> 
> So, let's talk about some real use-case and then we can decide if throttling
> makes sense here. If we decide to allow throttling in such cases, I would rather
> do it in memcg code i.e. somehow inform memcg code that this is THP allocation
> and can be throttled.

Hi Shakeel,

Thanks for the detailed review.

Honestly I don't have a real use-case. I ran into this while testing THP
under memory.high, so it's a semantic inconsistency I noticed rather than
a workload I'm fixing. 

The thing that seemed off is just that memory.high enforcement depends on
the folio order the workload happens to fault in - order-0 gets
throttled, THP under the default THP settings doesn't - which the user
has no control over. 

I don't have a firm view on the right semantics here either, and I think
you're right that that's the thing to pin down first. Whether the
order-dependence above is worth doing something about, or whether it's
acceptable for large folios to skip memory.high, I don't have a strong
opinion on - I'm happy to go with whatever the discussion settles on, and
if it's working as intended, that's just as useful to know.

And if it does turn out to be worth throttling, I'd be happy to rework it.

Thanks,
Qinyun Tan

review_comments.author: Luiz Capitulino
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that the patch's assumption about PMD page support is incorrect, as some architectures like x86 have conditional support and may lack PSE bit presence even on 64-bit systems; he also pointed out that has_transparent_hugepage() has different semantics on certain architectures and should not be used to gate all THP support.
sentiment_signals: pointed out semantic differences in has_transparent_hugepage()
review_comments.raw_body:
No :)

The architectures that have conditional PMD page support (ie. discovered
at run-time via has_transparent_hugepage()) are x86, s390, powerpc and
mips.

For x86 for example, even on 64-bit there are cases where the PSE bit
may not be present (eg. some errata and by hypervisor CPUID masking).

That being said, the main goal of the series is that
has_transparent_hugepage() is overloaded: it has different semantics on
those architectures and is used to gate all THP support (which is not
the right thing to do for mTHP).
